keep: The idea is named in the first two sentences: work is force moved through distance, power is how fast, so a slow lift takes the same energy at less power.

The rule is stated in words and worked with real numbers from the brief: 500 kg at 0.2 m/s is 4905 N, 49,050 J over 10 m, 50 s, 981 W; at 0.1 m/s the same 49.05 kJ over 100 s at 490.5 W. P = F × v is derived from work per second, not asserted.

The force on the rope is tied to Newton's laws: steady speed means balanced forces, so the rope pulls the weight. The recall of Vectors (only the part along the movement counts) is a one-line reminder and a puzzle, not a re-teach.

Each brief misconception has a wrong pick: power and work confused (screen 4, 9810 W), kinetic energy where power was asked (screen 13, 10 J), the mass used for the weight (screens 12 and 13), and newton-metres against a moment (screen 14, 50 J). The newton meter slip is a common mistake in practice.
The ledger's first bar is electrical power in, the volts × amps Dan knows, with efficiency as useful out ÷ in, and the 80% is labelled an example.
Fourteen screens alternate SHOW (1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11) and DO (2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12) and end on two mixed puzzles (13, 14). Lifting machines get one SHOW and one DO, as the brief decided.

The analogy is from his trade, two heaters on one meter, and reproduces the main result (same kWh, half the kW, twice the time); its break is the honest one, that a heater's energy is not stored to come back.
fix: Footnotes: renumber the text's [^n] to the research numbers in sources: [^2] energy transfer, [^4] the joule, [^3] power, [^10] the moment.
False absolute: 'volts × amps' for the motor's power in is only true for DC; Dan knows an AC motor brings in the power factor (AC circuits). Say volts × amps for a DC motor.

False absolute: 'a slow lift takes the same energy as a quick one' is true of the energy into the load, not of what the supply gives when efficiency shifts with speed. Say the same energy into the load, in the opening and in the bold takeaway.

Causal step skipped: 'The stored energy is the load's weight × its height, mgh' gives no reason. Say it is the work done raising it, the weight mg times the height h, and name it potential energy there.

Causal step skipped: ½mv² was got only from a free fall, so it reads as a falling-body fact. Derive it for any steady net force from rest from the two rules of Newton's laws, F = ma and v² = u² + 2as with u = 0, then apply it to the fall, and name it kinetic energy.
Causal step skipped: the chain block's 'works out as MA over VR' does not show the regrouping. Write the work out ÷ work in as load × its distance over effort × its distance, then regroup.
Brief shows the effect without its cause: the halved bars are explained by the doubled time. Add 'in twice the time' so the graph's 100 s is part of what to watch.
Practice common mistake 'the power all goes into height and losses' muddles the load's power with the motor's. Say the power into the load all goes into height.
Terms: keep to three marked terms (work, power, efficiency). Potential energy and kinetic energy are named in plain words once they are explained, without markers.
